80757.subject: Crypto’s Weakest Link
80757.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

Last Friday, [reports started surfacing](https://x.com/tanuki42_/status/2108527923766399243?s=20) of a multimillion-dollar hack where wallets were seemingly drained out of the blue across Tron, EVM, and Bitcoin. Over time, it became clear that the root cause of these hacks was a [supply chain attack on Southeast Asian Ledger hardware wallet reseller, CryptoBilis](https://x.com/Ledger/status/2109331538072494364). The reseller, which allegedly saw a change in ownership earlier this year, was [distributing modified wallets](https://x.com/magicaltux/status/2108583893809201216?s=46) with a CPU chip able to read a user’s seed phrase off its screen and transmit this data wirelessly using an embedded eSIM. While the issue seemed contained regionally initially, reports started surfacing of similar modifications on wallets purchased from resellers in the [EU](https://x.com/MagicalTux/status/2109670705147367744) and in [Singapore](https://x.com/MagicalTux/status/2109916873689280900%5C), suggesting the supply chain attack may be more widespread.

While most of the industry’s security spending over the past few years has gone toward auditing smart contracts, the Ledger incident, which is estimated to have drained just under $100M, is a clear example of attackers increasingly finding exploits that bypass smart contracts entirely. In late July and early August of this year, numerous Coldcard wallets were exploited due to weak randomness associated with generated seed phrases. This attack, which also targeted hardware wallets, [led to just over $100M in stolen funds](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/the-largest-hardware-wallet-exploit-of-2026-inside-the-usd-116-million-coldcard-hack). 

Social engineering attacks, which have been a dominant attack vector for North Korean entities, have produced some of the year’s largest hacks. Drift, a perps protocol on Solana, was hacked in April of this year for close to [$300M by North Korea-linked groups](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/north-korean-hackers-attack-drift-protocol-in-285-million-heist), following close to half a year of rapport building with the team. Posing as a trading firm, attackers were able to compromise key permissions to the protocol that allowed them to eventually drain user vaults using a worthless token as collateral. Resolv, a stablecoin protocol, experienced an [exploit following a similar logic](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/lessons-from-the-resolv-hack/) a few weeks earlier. A third-party breach led to the compromise of a contractor’s GitHub credentials, allowing attackers to mint unbacked stablecoins and drain close to $25M from the platform.
